name: Early Signals of Dementia
title: Early Signals of Dementia
answer: Early signals of dementia are subtle changes in memory, language, orientation and behaviour that appear years before a formal diagnosis, and the field studies them through cognitive testing, imaging, fluid biomarkers and digital behaviour traces. The aim is to detect a trajectory rather than a single event, since conditions such as Alzheimer's disease develop slowly and a single test rarely settles the question. Work here spans neurology, psychiatry, geriatrics and data science, and it overlaps with the wider effort to build models that support clinical judgement rather than replace it.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Early signals of dementia are subtle changes in memory, language, orientation and behaviour that appear years before a formal diagnosis, and the field studies them through cognitive testing, imaging, fluid biomarkers and digital behaviour traces. The aim is to detect a trajectory rather than a single event, since conditions such as Alzheimer's disease develop slowly and a single test rarely settles the question. Work here spans neurology, psychiatry, geriatrics and data science, and it overlaps with the wider effort to build models that support clinical judgement rather than replace it.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The data comes from memory clinics, cohort studies and research registries: structural and functional MRI, PET amyloid and tau imaging, cerebrospinal fluid and blood biomarker panels, genetic data, and longitudinal cognitive scores. Increasingly it also comes from cheaper sources such as speech recordings, keyboard and touchscreen interaction logs, wearable sleep and activity data, and electronic health records. These streams are heterogeneous, collected at different intervals and under different protocols, so most of the engineering effort goes into harmonisation, missing data handling and secure storage rather than into the models themselves.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A common pattern is to combine a small number of well validated predictors, such as age, APOE genotype, hippocampal volume and a memory score, into a risk model, then test whether adding a newer signal improves prediction. Machine learning is used for image segmentation, for classifying scans as typical or atypical, and for extracting features from speech and behaviour that a clinician would not score by hand. Validation is the hard part: models trained on one cohort often lose accuracy on another, so external validation, calibration and reporting of confidence intervals matter more than headline accuracy. The site tracks 1,000 medical AI models, and only a fraction of those in this area have been tested prospectively in a real clinic.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: A prediction about future cognitive decline is sensitive personal data, and in many jurisdictions it counts as health data with strict rules on consent, storage and secondary use. Blood and imaging biomarkers raise questions about what a person is told when a result is uncertain, and about insurance and employment consequences that follow from a recorded risk. Speech and interaction data add a further layer, because voice can identify a speaker and behaviour logs can reveal much more than memory.Nothing here is medical or legal advice, and any clinical use belongs with qualified professionals.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward blood based biomarkers and low cost digital markers that could be collected outside specialist centres, with AI used to decide who needs a full workup. That raises the practical question of what a primary care clinician does with a risk score when no disease modifying treatment is available, and how to avoid unnecessary alarm. Research is also moving toward multi modal models that combine imaging, fluid and behavioural data, and toward continuous monitoring rather than one off assessment. The unresolved issues are fairness across languages, education levels and ancestries, and the evidence needed before a model is used on anyone outside a study.
